criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Determine whether every dimension in the taxonomy captures a fundamentally different type of distinction. If two dimensions are really just different values on the same underlying axis (for example 'Bug Reports' and 'Feature Requests' are both values of 'Issue Type'), the taxonomy fails this criterion.
criteria.reason: The output defines multiple distinct taxonomy dimensions (e.g., Authentication and Session Security Policy, Data Protection Architecture, Payment Integration Strategy, Bike Location and Discovery Strategy, Notification Delivery and Scheduling Strategy, Operational Observability Strategy, Data Access and Persistence Strategy) that generally correspond to different architectural distinction types rather than repeating the same axis. Within each dimension, the values appear to be different options on that axis (e.g., session termination vs inactivity timeout vs verification-code validity under dimension 1). However, the test case does not provide the Input taxonomy dimensions to compare against, so the required checks for one-to-one correspondence between Input and Actual Output dimensions (steps 1, 3, and 4) cannot be fully validated. Additionally, some descriptions overlap conceptually (e.g., Notification Delivery vs Operational Observability both involve event propagation/subscription), which could indicate partial axis overlap, though the output attempts to separate them via distinct concerns.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Determine whether the dimension names and descriptions are clear enough that a labeler could classify documents accurately without ambiguity, and whether each description explains what kind of documents fall along that dimension.
criteria.reason: The actual output provides multiple clearly named dimensions (e.g., “Authentication and Session Security Policy”, “Payment Integration Strategy”, “Bike Location and Discovery Strategy”, “Notification Delivery and Scheduling Strategy”, etc.) with consistent, unambiguous naming that would map to the input request for a taxonomy. For each dimension, the descriptions and value descriptions give explicit inclusion criteria (e.g., session termination methods and verification-code validity for dimension 1; adapter/facade/strategy mechanisms for dimension 3; radius-constrained geospatial search and real-time tracking for dimension 4). Boundaries are generally well stated as “distinct from” other concerns (e.g., notification delivery separate from location computation; authentication distinct from general data protection architecture; data protection separate from authentication/sessions/integrations), supporting step 3. However, the input only says “Generate the taxonomy…” without providing any dimension names or explicit criteria to compare against, so step 1 and step 4 (consistency between Input and Actual Output) cannot be fully validated; additionally, some relations introduce cross-cutting co-occurrence rationales that could slightly blur boundaries (e.g., notifications vs location, dashboards vs notification delivery), though the descriptions still attempt to keep concerns separate.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: Determine whether the taxonomy captures all major axes of variation implied by the stated use case, or whether recurring kinds of distinctions are missing. Judge against the use case in the input, not against topics the use case excludes.
criteria.reason: The response provides a multi-axis taxonomy for labeling user intent, with distinct major areas that plausibly match the implied scope of a bike-sharing system (e.g., Authentication and Session Security Policy, Bike Location and Discovery Strategy, Payment Integration Strategy, Notification Delivery and Scheduling Strategy, Observability, Data Protection, and Data Access). However, the input only states a generic instruction to “generate the taxonomy” without specifying concrete variation criteria or axes of variation for user intent, so steps 1–4 (verifying all major axes are represented, checking for gaps, and confirming consistent recurrence) cannot be reliably validated against the input’s requirements. Additionally, while the taxonomy includes many architectural concerns, it is not clearly tied to “user intent in the conversation” (e.g., no explicit intent categories like troubleshooting, booking/rental actions, billing questions, or location requests), suggesting potential mismatch with the stated use case.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Determine whether every dimension serves the stated use case. Dimensions that exist in the abstract but do not help achieve the use case in the input should lower the score.
criteria.reason: The input asks for a taxonomy to label user intent in a conversation, but the actual output provides architectural dimensions (e.g., Data Protection Architecture, Authentication and Session Security Policy, Payment Integration Strategy, Bike Location and Discovery Strategy, Notification Delivery and Scheduling Strategy, Operational Observability Strategy, Data Access and Persistence Strategy). These dimensions do not directly map to user-intent labeling requirements. While some dimensions are internally justified (e.g., location vs notification separation), they are irrelevant to the stated use case. The output also adds many abstract, domain-specific concerns not evidenced by any input needs for intent categories, so the set of dimensions does not collectively cover the requested intent-labeling use case.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: Determine whether the taxonomy contains an 'Other', 'Miscellaneous', or similarly vague catch-all dimension, or whether every dimension is specific enough that a document clearly belongs or does not belong.
criteria.reason: The actual output defines multiple specific taxonomy dimensions (e.g., Authentication and Session Security Policy, Bike Location and Discovery Strategy, Payment Integration Strategy, Notification Delivery and Scheduling Strategy) with clearly labeled values. There is no introduction of any vague catch-all category such as 'Other' or 'Miscellaneous'. Since the input does not specify any catch-all dimension, the output correctly avoids one and assigns each document to a specific, unambiguous dimension with matching scope (e.g., session timeouts under dimension 1, geospatial radius search under dimension 4, observer-based notifications under dimension 5).

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Determine whether each dimension is truly an axis of variation rather than a single value dressed up as an axis. A dimension named 'Bug Reports' might really be one value on an 'Issue Type' axis that also includes feature requests and questions.
criteria.reason: The actual output defines multiple named dimensions (e.g., Authentication and Session Security Policy, Bike Location and Discovery Strategy, Notification Delivery and Scheduling Strategy) and each dimension has multiple values, satisfying the requirement that dimensions correspond to true axes with variation rather than single fixed instances. For instance, dimension_id 1 includes four distinct authentication/session variants (immediate logout, inactivity timeout, biometric with deletion, verification-code validity), and dimension_id 4 includes two different location/discovery strategies (radius-constrained search and real-time tracking). The output does not appear to re-label a single value as an axis; instead, it reframes each input-intended axis into broader categories with multiple value options. One minor limitation is that the input is generic (“Generate the taxonomy…”) and does not explicitly list expected dimensions, so alignment is inferred from the output’s internal structure rather than directly verified against stated input dimensions.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Determine whether every document in the input can be placed along at least one dimension of the taxonomy. Penalize documents that fit no dimension's axis of variation, naming the document themes that are left uncovered.
criteria.reason: The actual output maps many of the input documents to taxonomy dimensions: end-to-end encryption to Data Protection (dimension 2.1), proximity radius search and location-based tracking to Bike Location and Discovery (dimension 4.1/4.2), payment adapter/facade/strategy to Payment Integration (dimension 3.1-3.3), observer-based bike status/usage notifications to Notification Delivery (dimension 5.1/5.2), and logout/inactivity/biometric/verification-code timing to Authentication and Session Security (dimension 1.1-1.4). However, several input themes are not clearly covered: the event-driven architecture for 'bike registered' triggering immediate removal from available list is not explicitly mapped to any dimension/axis, the state machine for navigation/scanning/unlocking/rental duration management is not mapped, the builder pattern for usage history reports is not mapped, and the timeout/token-expiration/30-minute TTL aspects of verification code are only partially represented (only a 30-second validity is present, while the input includes 30-minute TTL and token expiration). Because these uncovered themes remain, the coverage check would require penalties.
